etymology: From a proper name combined with an English element, modelled on a French word, per the Oxford English Dictionary: Louis Pasteur (1822–1895), the French chemist and microbiologist. The OED records its earliest evidence in 1881, in the Pharmaceutical Journal & Transactions.
biblical_def: To pasteurize is to heat a food or drink, such as milk, juice or wine, gently enough to keep it and hot enough to kill the microbes that would spoil it or carry disease. The process is named for Louis Pasteur. During a summer holiday at Arbois in 1864, looking for a remedy for the souring of the local wines, he found that heating a young wine to about 50–60 °C for a short time was enough to kill the microbes. His work also supported the germ theory of disease, and his vaccines for rabies and anthrax are credited with saving millions of lives. Born to a Catholic family of a poor tanner, he was described by his son-in-law as having “absolute faith in God and in Eternity.” The Christian observation: the microbe was there before Pasteur saw it, and the law of Moses already commanded washing and separation as defences against uncleanness (Lev 11:32). Solomon names the calling of the man of science: “It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter” (Pro 25:2). “The works of the LORD are great, sought out of all them that have pleasure therein” (Psa 111:2).
webster_summary: To heat a food or drink enough to kill spoiling and disease-carrying microbes; from Louis Pasteur, who found the method for wine in 1864 (OED earliest 1881). The honour of kings is to search out a matter (Pro 25:2).
webster_full: PASTEURIZE, v.t. (from 1881, OED) To treat a food or beverage with mild heat in order to destroy disease-causing microorganisms and lengthen its keeping. From Louis Pasteur (1822–1895) + -ize.
History note: Pasteur’s method was first worked out for wine at Arbois in 1864 (Wikipedia, “Pasteurization”).
scriptures: Pro 25:2
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.
The works of the LORD are great, sought out of all them that have pleasure therein.

And upon whatsoever any of them, when they are dead, doth fall, it shall be unclean; whether it be any vessel of wood, or raiment, or skin, or sack, whatsoever vessel it be, wherein any work is done, it must be put into water, and it shall be unclean until the even; so it shall be cleansed.
Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities.
corruption_summary: Pasteur searched out God’s hidden works and saved millions; the corruption is the claim that science and faith are enemies, which his own life contradicts.
corruption_paragraphs: A common modern story casts the scientist as the man who replaced faith with evidence. Pasteur, one of the founders of modern microbiology, does not fit the story: his son-in-law recorded his absolute faith in God and eternity. To search out what God has concealed is, in Solomon’s words, the honour of kings (Pro 25:2).

The opposite error is to treat God’s gifts through medicine and food science with suspicion, as if seeking them were a lack of faith. Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1Ti 5:23). Means are not a rival to Providence; they are one of its instruments.
roots_summary: Louis Pasteur (1822–1895) → mild heating of wine, Arbois, 1864 → pasteurize (OED earliest 1881) → milk and other foods.
roots_lines: 1864: Pasteur finds that brief heating of young wine kills the microbes (Wikipedia)
Today: standard in the dairy and food-processing industries (Wikipedia)
usage: “Buy the pasteurized milk for the baby.”
The works of the LORD are great, sought out of all them that have pleasure therein. (Psa 111:2).

etymology: From a proper name, per the Oxford English Dictionary: André-Marie Ampère (1775–1836), the French physicist and mathematician. The OED records its earliest evidence in 1846, in a translation by E. West. An international convention at the 1881 International Exposition of Electricity made the ampere a standard unit.
biblical_def: The ampere, or amp, is the unit of electric current. It is named for André-Marie Ampère, one of the founders of classical electromagnetism, which he called electrodynamics. Largely self-taught, he became a member of the French Academy of Sciences and a professor at the École polytechnique and the Collège de France, coined the word solenoid, and contributed to the invention of the electrical telegraph. His mother was a devout Catholic, and he was raised in the Catholic faith alongside the science of the Enlightenment. In 1881 an international convention adopted the ampere as a standard unit of electrical measurement in recognition of his work. The Christian observation: the current measured in amperes was in the lightning before any man measured it. God asked Job, “Canst thou send lightnings, that they may go, and say unto thee, Here we are?” (Job 38:35). The man of science who learns to direct a little of that power is still a student of God’s works: “The works of the LORD are great, sought out of all them that have pleasure therein” (Psa 111:2). “The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork” (Psa 19:1).
webster_summary: The unit of electric current; named for André-Marie Ampère, a founder of electrodynamics (OED earliest 1846; adopted as a standard unit 1881). Canst thou send lightnings? (Job 38:35).
webster_full: AMPERE, n. (from 1846, OED) The SI unit of electric current. Shortened to amp. From André-Marie Ampère (1775–1836).
History note: established as a standard unit by an international convention at the 1881 International Exposition of Electricity (Wikipedia).
scriptures: Canst thou send lightnings, that they may go, and say unto thee, Here we are?
The works of the LORD are great, sought out of all them that have pleasure therein.
Psa 19:1
The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
corruption_summary: We meter electricity in amperes and forget the Lord of the lightning; mastery of a force is not ownership of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Electric power is so ordinary now that a child flips a switch without a thought of where the current comes from. The danger is not the switch but the forgetting. A people that commands lightning in its walls is tempted to think it no longer needs to ask God for anything.
God’s question to Job still stands (Job 38:35). Ampère learned to measure a force God made, and the heavens still declare whose handiwork it is (Psa 19:1).
roots_summary: André-Marie Ampère (1775–1836), electrodynamics → ampere (OED earliest 1846) → standard unit by convention, 1881 → SI unit of current.
roots_lines: 1846: OED’s earliest evidence, translation by E. West
1881: adopted as a standard unit at the International Exposition of Electricity (Wikipedia)
usage: “That circuit is rated for fifteen amperes; don’t run the heater on it.”
The heavens declare the glory of God. (Psa 19:1).

etymology: From a proper name, per the Oxford English Dictionary: Charles Macintosh (1766–1843), the Scottish chemist. The OED records its earliest evidence in 1835, in the Analyst. Writers added a k to his name, and the spelling mackintosh is now standard.
biblical_def: A mackintosh, or mac, is a raincoat of waterproof fabric. Charles Macintosh, born in Glasgow, began as a clerk, studied chemistry in his spare time, and before he was twenty left the clerkship to study under Joseph Black at the University of Edinburgh and to manufacture chemicals. Experimenting with naphtha, he found that it would dissolve natural rubber, and he patented a waterproof fabric made by cementing two thicknesses of cloth together with the rubber between them. The Mackintosh brand introduced the raincoat in 1824. It has been claimed that the surgeon James Syme invented the material first and Macintosh copied and patented it. The Christian observation: a raincoat is a small mercy against the weather, and Scripture uses shelter from rain for a far greater one. “And there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain” (Isa 4:6). The same God “prepareth rain for the earth” (Psa 147:8). And Christ’s parable makes the real test of a man’s life the storm: “the rain descended, and the floods came… and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock” (Mat 7:25).
webster_summary: A raincoat of rubberized waterproof cloth; named for Charles Macintosh, who patented the fabric (OED earliest 1835; garment introduced 1824). A covert from storm and from rain (Isa 4:6).
webster_full: MACKINTOSH (also macintosh, mac), n. (from 1835, OED) A raincoat of waterproof, originally rubberized, cloth. From Charles Macintosh (1766–1843).
History note: waterproof fabric of two cloths cemented with naphtha-dissolved rubber; the raincoat introduced in 1824 (Wikipedia).
scriptures: Isa 4:6
And there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain.
Who covereth the heaven with clouds, who prepareth rain for the earth, who maketh grass to grow upon the mountains.
Mat 7:25
And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.
corruption_summary: A coat keeps off the rain but not the storm Christ spoke of; the error is to trust outer coverings when only the foundation holds.
corruption_paragraphs: Men are good at inventing coverings. Macintosh’s fabric kept a man dry, and that is a real good. But the storms of life and judgment are not turned by a better coat.

Christ told of two houses in one storm. What decided between them was not their outward finish but their foundation (Mat 7:25). The refuge Isaiah promised is God’s own tabernacle (Isa 4:6), and the only foundation that stands is Christ.
roots_summary: Charles Macintosh (1766–1843), naphtha and rubber → waterproof double cloth → raincoat, 1824 → mackintosh (OED earliest 1835), with an added k.
roots_lines: Glasgow clerk turned chemist; studied under Joseph Black at Edinburgh (Wikipedia)
usage: “Take your mac; the clouds are coming in off the river.”
A covert from storm and from rain. (Isa 4:6).

etymology: From a proper name, per the Oxford English Dictionary: Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin (1838–1917), the German general and inventor of the rigid airship. The OED records its earliest evidence in 1896, in the Washington Post.
biblical_def: A zeppelin is a rigid airship: a long frame covered in fabric and lifted by gas-filled cells inside it. The word is named for Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin, a German general whose name became synonymous with airships, which dominated long-distance flight until the 1930s. His interest began, by his own later account, in America. In 1863 he took leave to observe the Union’s Army of the Potomac in Virginia, and afterward, travelling in Minnesota, he made his first ascent in a balloon with the itinerant balloonist John Steiner at St. Paul. On 2 July 1900 he made the first flight of his LZ 1 over Lake Constance; it stayed up for twenty minutes and was damaged on landing. The Christian observation: men had long watched the clouds before they rode them, and Scripture gives the clouds to God as His chariot: He “maketh the clouds his chariot: who walketh upon the wings of the wind” (Psa 104:3). Every human flight is borrowed lift. The higher promise is to those who wait on the LORD: “they shall mount up with wings as eagles” (Isa 40:31). And a man may plan his voyage, but “the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9).
webster_summary: A rigid airship, named for Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin, who first rose in a balloon at St. Paul after observing the Civil War in Virginia (OED earliest 1896; first flight 1900). He maketh the clouds his chariot (Psa 104:3).
webster_full: ZEPPELIN, n. (from 1896, OED) A large rigid airship with a covered framework containing gas cells. From Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin (1838–1917).
History note: observer with the Army of the Potomac in Virginia, 1863; first flight of LZ 1, 2 July 1900 (Wikipedia, “Ferdinand von Zeppelin”).
scriptures: Who layeth the beams of his chambers in the waters: who maketh the clouds his chariot: who walketh upon the wings of the wind:
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
Pro 16:9
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
corruption_summary: Man learned to ride the clouds God made His chariot; the temptation of every age of flight is to think the sky now belongs to us.
corruption_paragraphs: The airship was a triumph, and for a generation it ruled long-distance flight. Then its age ended. Human mastery of the air has moved on many times since, and each step brings the same temptation: to look down from a height and imagine we have climbed beyond the need of God.

Scripture keeps the clouds in God’s hand (Psa 104:3) and puts the true rising elsewhere, in the strength given to those who wait on the LORD (Isa 40:31). A man devises his way; the LORD directs his steps (Pro 16:9).
roots_summary: Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin (1838–1917) → balloon ascent at St. Paul, 1863 → LZ 1, 1900 → zeppelin (OED earliest 1896) → any rigid airship.
roots_lines: 1863: observer with the Union’s Army of the Potomac in Virginia; first balloon ascent at St. Paul, Minnesota (Wikipedia)
2 July 1900: first flight of LZ 1 over Lake Constance (Wikipedia)
usage: “Grandpa said he saw a zeppelin drift over the river as a boy.”
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps. (Pro 16:9).

etymology: From a proper name, per the Oxford English Dictionary: John Batterson Stetson (1830–1906), the American hat maker. The OED records its earliest evidence from around 1900.
biblical_def: A Stetson is a broad-brimmed, high-crowned hat of the kind worn by cowboys, and loosely any cowboy hat. John B. Stetson, born in Orange, New Jersey, was one of twelve children of a hatter who taught him the trade. In 1865 he founded the John B. Stetson Company in Philadelphia to make hats suited to the needs of Westerners, and sent samples of his “Boss of the Plains” style to dealers in the West, who were soon flooded with orders. His company became one of the largest hat makers in the world. Guided by Baptist principles, he believed that by providing for his employees he would lend stability to their lives, and he offered benefits when most employers did not. His philanthropy helped fund Temple University and Stetson University, a YMCA, and a homeless shelter and soup kitchen in Philadelphia. The Christian observation: Paul’s word to masters is the rule Stetson tried to keep: “Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven” (Col 4:1). “The labourer is worthy of his reward” (1Ti 5:18), and “Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it” (Pro 3:27).
webster_summary: A broad-brimmed, high-crowned cowboy hat; from John B. Stetson, a Philadelphia hat maker guided by Baptist principles (OED around 1900; company founded 1865). Masters, give that which is just and equal (Col 4:1).
webster_full: STETSON, n. (from around 1900, OED) A broad-brimmed felt hat with a high crown, associated with the American West. From John B. Stetson (1830–1906).
History note: the John B. Stetson Company, Philadelphia, founded 1865; the “Boss of the Plains” style (Wikipedia).
scriptures: Col 4:1
Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven.
For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward.
Pro 3:27
Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it.
corruption_summary: Stetson built a great company and cared for his workers because he answered to a Master in heaven; the error is to think a business owes its people only the wage the market will bear.
corruption_paragraphs: Employers in Stetson’s trade expected workers to drift from shop to shop, and treated them as interchangeable. Stetson, by his own Baptist principles, did the opposite: he provided for his workers so that their lives would be stable. That is Paul’s rule for masters (Col 4:1).

A business run only for its owner treats the labourer as a cost. Scripture calls him worthy of his reward (1Ti 5:18) and tells the man with the power to do good not to withhold it (Pro 3:27). The Christian employer is a steward, not merely a buyer of hours.
roots_summary: John B. Stetson (1830–1906), hatter’s son → John B. Stetson Company, Philadelphia, 1865 → “Boss of the Plains” → Stetson (OED around 1900).
roots_lines: 1865: founds the John B. Stetson Company in Philadelphia (Wikipedia)
“Boss of the Plains”: the style that made his name in the West (Wikipedia)
usage: “He took off his Stetson when the preacher stood up.”
The labourer is worthy of his reward. (1Ti 5:18).

etymology: From a proper name combined with knife, per the Oxford English Dictionary: James Bowie (1796–1836). The OED records its earliest evidence in 1830, in the Daily National Intelligencer of Washington, D.C.
biblical_def: A Bowie knife is a large fixed-blade sheath knife with a crossguard and a clip point. The pattern was created by Rezin Bowie for his brother James, who became famous for using a large knife at the Sandbar Fight of 1827, a duel on a sandbar in the Mississippi River across from Natchez, the only documented fight in which he used it. James Bowie was a military officer, landowner and slave trader who played a prominent role in the Texas Revolution and died at the Battle of the Alamo in 1836. Stories about him as a fighter and frontiersman, both real and invented, made him a folk hero. The Christian observation: Scripture neither romanticizes the blade nor forbids it. Christ told His disciples, “he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one” (Luk 22:36), and the magistrate “beareth not the sword in vain” (Rom 13:4). But He also said, “Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52). A frontier legend that mixes courage with slave-trading and duelling is a reminder to honour what was right and refuse to honour what was sin.
webster_summary: A large fixed-blade sheath knife with a crossguard and clip point; made by Rezin Bowie for his brother James after the Sandbar Fight of 1827 (OED earliest 1830). They that take the sword shall perish with the sword (Mat 26:52).
webster_full: BOWIE KNIFE, n. (from 1830, OED) A large fixed-blade knife with a crossguard and a clip point, carried in a sheath. From James Bowie (1796–1836) + knife.
History note: created by Rezin Bowie; made famous by the Sandbar Fight near Natchez, 1827 (Wikipedia, “Bowie knife”).
scriptures: Then said he unto them, But now, he that hath a purse, let him take it, and likewise his scrip: and he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
corruption_summary: Frontier legend turned Bowie into a simple hero; the honest record includes the duel and the slave trade, and Scripture asks us to honour courage without excusing sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Folk heroes are made by leaving things out. Bowie’s legend keeps the knife, the frontier and the Alamo, and quietly drops the slave trading and the duelling. A Christian reading of history does not tear down every hero, but it will not baptize the whole man to keep the story tidy.

Scripture’s teaching on the blade is balanced: lawful defence and lawful justice are permitted (Luk 22:36; Rom 13:4), and the man who lives by the sword is warned (Mat 26:52). A knife is a tool. The question is always the hand and the heart that hold it.
roots_summary: James Bowie (1796–1836) → Sandbar Fight near Natchez, 1827 → knife made by Rezin Bowie → Bowie knife (OED earliest 1830).
roots_lines: 1827: the Sandbar Fight, on the Mississippi across from Natchez (Wikipedia)
1836: James Bowie dies at the Alamo (Wikipedia)
usage: “He kept a Bowie knife in his pack for cleaning game.”
All they that take the sword shall perish with the sword. (Mat 26:52).
